t: #4025 Minimize the Maximum Waiting Time at Synchronized Traffic Lights — Editorial
o: Every light shares one cycle of length `period`; light i is green during residues [0, lights[i]). A car with residue r waits 0 if r < lights[i], else period − r. Since more green time is never worse, only the maximum green duration L = max(lights) matters: a car can avoid waiting iff some light has lights[i] > r, i.e. iff r < L. Every other car inevitably waits period − r regardless of assignment. Hence the optimal penalty is simply the maximum of period − r over cars with r ≥ L (or 0 if none). All three examples confirm this: e.g. Example 1 has L = 3 and residues 5 and 3 ≥ 3, giving max(3, 5) = 5.
k: Assignment flexibility is irrelevant: only the longest green phase L = max(lights) matters, since a bigger green window dominates.
A car with residue r waits iff r ≥ L, and then its wait is exactly period − r no matter which light it uses.
So the answer is max(period − (t mod period)) over arrivals with residue ≥ L, else 0 — computable in one pass.

a.n: Approach 1: Binary Search on the Penalty
a.i: Binary search the answer P. Penalty P is achievable iff every car's residue r satisfies r < L (zero wait possible) or period − r ≤ P (its forced wait fits within P). Feasibility is monotone in P, so binary search finds the minimum.
s: Let L = max(lights). Collect the distinct residues of all arrivals.
can(P): true iff every residue r has r < L or period − r ≤ P.
Binary search P over [0, period − 1] for the minimal feasible value.
a.t: O(m log period + n) — n arrivals hashed into ≤ period distinct residues, then ~31 feasibility checks over them.

a.i: From the dominance argument, each car's minimum possible wait is fixed: 0 if its residue r < L, otherwise period − r. The penalty of the best assignment is the max of these per-car minima, computed in a single pass with no search.
s: For each arrival, r = t % period.
If r ≥ L, candidate = period − r; track the maximum candidate.
Return the tracked maximum, or 0 if no car had r ≥ L.
a.t: O(n + m) — one pass over lights for the max and one pass over arrivals.

w: Always present the greedy formula; the binary search version is mainly useful if the problem were extended (e.g., cars could be delayed to later cycles, or lights chosen adaptively). Pitfalls: thinking cars interact or queues matter (they explicitly don't), boundary r == lights[i] (that's red — wait applies, since green is r < lights[i]), and off-by-one on the binary search upper bound period − 1. Edge cases: all cars arrive during green → 0; a single light forces every late-residue car's full wait (Example 3). Follow-up: what if each light could be shifted by an offset, or cars had deadlines?
